puzzle.hint: There is exactly one spy among the players.

statements.speaker: Player A
statements.text: at least one of the following is true: (1) at least 2 of Player A and Player B are knaves; (2) Player A and Player B have the same role.

statements.speaker: Player B
statements.text: it is not the case that (at least 0 of Player A and Player F are spies).

statements.speaker: Player C
statements.text: it is not the case that (at most 1 of Player A, Player B, Player C, Player E, and Player F are spies).

statements.speaker: Player D
statements.text: it is not the case that (Player B and Player C have the same role).

statements.speaker: Player E
statements.text: it is not the case that (Player A is a knight).

statements.speaker: Player F
statements.text: at most 2 of Player C, Player D, Player E, and Player F are knights.

fields.text: Player B and Player C make statements that are logically false, making them knaves or the spy. Player E's statement evaluates to true only if Player A is a knight. Analyzing the truth values and the single spy constraint yields Player E as the spy, with A and D as knights, and B, C, and F as knaves.

B's statement is always false, so B is knave or spy; assuming B knave works. D must be knave to make B and C same role, forcing C knave. With one spy, A fits as spy. E's false statement makes E knave. F must be knight to keep his statement true. All roles satisfy constraints.

B and C must be knaves because their statements are impossible to be true. A cannot be knight or knave, so A is the single spy. D’s statement is false (B and C are both knaves), so D is a knave. E’s statement is true (A is not knight), making E a knight. F’s statement is always true (at most two of C,D,E,F are knights), so F must be a knight. All constraints satisfied.
Agent-2 correctly identifies Player A as the single spy.
Agent-3 contradicts its own solution by claiming Player A is a knave.
B and C statements are always false, so B can be spy and C knave. This forces D true, E true, F true, making A's statement false, thus A knave.
Agent-1 claims A is spy, but logical analysis shows A must be knave.

B’s statement is always false, so B must be spy. C’s statement is also always false, making C a knave. D’s statement then true, so D is knight. E’s statement false, so E is knave. F’s statement true, so F is knight. A cannot be knight (statement would be false) and cannot be spy (already used by B), leaving only knave, which satisfies all constraints.

Player B and C make statements that are always false, making them knaves. Player A is the single spy. Player D's statement is false, making D a knave. Player E's statement is true since A is not a knight, making E a knight. Player F's statement is true, making F a knight.

B and C statements are always false, so they are knaves or the spy. Assigning A as the spy makes B and C knaves. D then lies (knave). E’s claim that A is not a knight is true, so E is a knight. F’s at‑most‑2‑knights claim is true with only E and F as knights, so F is a knight. All statements match roles.

Assuming B’s claim means ‘neither A nor F is spy’, the only consistent role set has A as the sole spy. Then B and C’s false statements force B and C to be knaves. D’s statement is false so D is knave. E’s claim true, so E is knight. F’s statement ‘at most 2 of C,D,E,F are knights’ is true, so F must be knight. All constraints satisfied.
Both agents correctly deduce that Player B's statement is false, making Player B a knave.
All analyses show B's statement is always false, so B must be a knave.

B’s statement is always false; if B were spy, the unique spy position would force contradictions with F’s statement and A’s knightness. Thus B must lie, i.e., be knave. Both agent‑1 and agent‑2 propose B knave, matching this deduction.

Player B and C make false statements, making them knaves. Player A is the single spy. Player D's statement is false, making D a knave. Player E's statement is true since A is not a knight, making E a knight. Player F's statement is true as there are exactly 2 knights among C, D, E, and F, making F a knight.

B’s statement is always false, so B is a knave. C’s statement is also always false, making C a knave. D’s claim that B and C have the same role is false, so D is a knave. E’s claim that A is not a knight is true, so E is a knight. F’s at‑most‑2‑knights condition holds with only E and F as knights, so F is a knight. With one spy remaining, A must be the spy.

B’s statement is always false, so B must be knave. C’s statement is also always false, so C is knave. If the spy were B or C we get contradictions on A’s statement. Making A the spy satisfies A’s false statement. D’s statement is false (B and C are both knaves), so D is knave. E’s statement is true because A is not a knight, so E is a knight. F’s statement is true with only E and F as knights, so F is a knight.
All agents correctly deduce that Player C is a knave.
All analyses show C's statement is always false, making C a knave.
Both agents propose the same role distribution as ours; evaluating each statement confirms C must be a knave.

Player B and C make false statements making them knaves. Player A is the sole spy. Player D's claim that B and C share roles is false, making D a knave. Player E's statement that A is not a knight is true, making E a knight. Player F's statement holds true with E and F as the only knights.

B's statement is always false, so B is a knave. C's statement is also always false, making C a knave. D's claim that B and C share a role is false, so D is a knave. E's claim that A is not a knight is true, so E is a knight. F's at‑most‑2‑knights condition holds with only E and F as knights, so F is a knight. With one spy left, A must be the spy.

B and C’s statements are always false, so they are knaves or the spy. If B were spy, A’s statement would be false, forcing A knave and E knight, leaving D knight; F’s statement would then be true if F were knave, impossible. Thus B cannot be spy, so B is knave. Similarly C must be knave. With B and C knaves, only A can be spy to satisfy A’s false statement. Then E’s statement is true (A not knight) → E knight. D’s statement is false (B and C same role) → D knave. F’s statement is true (exactly two knights among C,D,E,F) → F knight. All conditions satisfied with a single spy.
Both peer agents correctly agree that since Player B and Player C are both knaves, they have the same role, making Player D's statement false and Player D a knave.
All analyses show B and C are knaves, making D's claim that they share a role false, so D must be a knave.

If spy is A, then B and C are knaves, making D lie about B and C having same role, so D is knave. This satisfies all statements and yields a consistent assignment. The same assignment matches both agents’ solutions.

Player B and C make false statements, making them knaves. Player A is the single spy. Player D lies about B and C sharing a role, making D a knave. Player E's statement is true because A is not a knight, making E a knight. Player F's statement holds true with E and F as the only knights.

B and C statements are always false, so they are knaves. D says B and C share a role, which is false, making D a knave. E’s claim that A is not a knight is true, so E is a knight. F’s at‑most‑2‑knights condition holds with only E and F as knights, so F is a knight. The only remaining role for A is spy, satisfying A’s false statement.

B’s statement is always false, so B is a knave. C’s statement is also always false, so C is a knave. With B and C both knaves, D’s statement "B and C have the same role" is true, making D a knave. A must be the lone spy to satisfy A’s ambiguous statement. E’s claim that A is not a knight is true, so E is a knight. F’s at‑most‑2‑knights condition is true with exactly two knights (E and F), so F is a knight.
Both agents correctly deduce E is a knight because A is the spy, making E's statement true.
All consistent solutions assign E as knight because A is the spy and E's statement is true.
Both agent-1 and agent-2 present solutions that satisfy all statements and the single‑spy rule; in each, Player E is a knight, matching the unique role deduced for E.

Player B and C make false statements, making them knaves. Player D lies about B and C sharing a role, making D a knave. Player E's statement is true since A is not a knight, making E a knight. Player F's at-most-2-knights statement holds with E and F as knights. Finally, Player A is the single spy, satisfying all constraints.

B and C statements are always false, so they are knaves. D's claim that B and C share a role is false, making D a knave. E says A is not a knight; this is true, so E is a knight. F's at‑most‑2‑knights condition holds with only E and F as knights, so F is a knight. The only remaining role for A is spy, satisfying A's false statement. All constraints are met.

B’s claim is false, so B is a knave. C’s claim is also false, so C is a knave. D says B and C have the same role; since they are both knaves the statement is false, so D is a knave. E’s statement that A is not a knight is true, making E a knight. F’s claim that at most two of C,D,E,F are knights holds with only E and F as knights, so F is a knight. A must be the lone spy to satisfy his ambiguous statement.
Both agents correctly deduce Player F is a knight since E and F are knights, satisfying F's statement.
All peers assign F as knight; his statement holds with exactly two knights (E and F).

B and C’s statements are always false, so they cannot be knights. If both are knaves, D’s claim that they differ is false, making D a knave. E’s statement is true when A is not a knight, so E must be a knight. With exactly one spy, A must be the spy. The only remaining knight is F, whose statement about at most two knights among C,D,E,F is true (there are two). Thus F is a knight, matching both peers’ solutions.

Player B and C make false statements, making them knaves. Player D's claim that B and C share roles is false, making D a knave. Player E's statement is true since A is not a knight, making E a knight. Player F's statement holds true with E and F as knights. Player A is the sole spy.

B and C's statements are always false, so they are knaves. D's claim that B and C share a role is false, making D a knave. E's statement that A is not a knight is true, so E is a knight. F's at‑most‑2‑knights condition holds with exactly E and F as knights, so F is a knight. The only remaining role for A is spy, satisfying his ambiguous statement.

B, C, and D must lie, so their statements are false. This forces B and C to be knaves (their claims about spies are impossible), and D’s claim that B and C have the same role is false, so D is also a knave. E’s statement is true when A is not a knight, making E a knight. F’s statement is true only if at most two of C, D, E, F are knights; with E and F knights it holds. The only remaining role is spy for A, satisfying all constraints.
